title: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
summary: Turn senior rust engineers in Berlin, remote ok, under 150k into a validated filter object, canonical IDs and an Elasticsearch bool query, then measure it per field and keep it fast.
outcomes: Explain why hard constraints belong in engine filters rather than in embedding similarity
Design a strict filter schema with enums, nullable range bounds, negation fields and residual text
Compile a normalized filter object into an Elasticsearch bool query without minimum_should_match bugs
Handle ambiguity, negation, unknown values and zero hits with validation and keyword fallback
Evaluate a parser with per-field exact match and slot precision, and budget its latency with caching

lessons.title: Why hard constraints need filters, not similarity

blocks.md: A recruiter types: **senior rust engineers in Berlin, remote ok, under 150k**. Read it as a database person would and it is five constraints plus a role: title is software engineer, seniority is senior, the skill list contains Rust, the candidate is in Berlin or open to remote work, and expected salary is below 150000. Each constraint is true or false for a profile. None of them is a matter of degree.

Two naive approaches fail in different ways.

1. **Embed the whole query** and return nearest neighbors. Similarity is a soft score over everything in the text. A Rust engineer in Berlin asking 165k looks almost identical to one asking 140k, because the number is a handful of tokens among many. Nothing enforces *below*.
2. **Keyword search** (BM25) on the raw text matches the literal strings `150k` and `Berlin`. A profile that writes München will not match Munich, and no keyword can express *less than*.

**LLM query parsing** (also called *self-querying* or *auto-retrieval*) splits the job. An LLM reads the query together with a description of the fields your index can filter on, and writes a **structured query**: a filter object with the hard constraints, plus a residual text string with whatever is left to rank by relevance. A search engine then enforces the filter exactly. This is a narrow case of **semantic parsing**, the older task of mapping language to an executable form such as SQL.

blocks.title: Query parsing pipeline in front of a search engine

scenes.caption: The user types free text. Nothing about it is structured yet: 150k, Berlin and senior are just tokens.
An LLM reads the query plus a description of the filterable fields and returns a filter object that must match a JSON schema (constrained decoding, from the prerequisite course).
Valid JSON is not yet valid meaning. Values are checked and mapped to canonical IDs from your own vocabularies: Berlin becomes geo:berlin.
A deterministic compiler, not the LLM, writes the engine query. Hard constraints become unscored filter clauses; leftover descriptive words become a scored text match.
If any step fails (timeout, unknown value, zero hits), the system still answers with plain keyword search on the raw text. Parsing should only ever make results better.

blocks.md: Both big retrieval frameworks ship this pattern. LangChain's `SelfQueryRetriever` describes each field with an `AttributeInfo` (name, description, type) and asks the LLM for a `StructuredQuery` with `query`, `filter` and an optional `limit`. Its filter language has comparators `eq ne gt gte lt lte contain like in nin` and operators `and or not`. LlamaIndex's `VectorIndexAutoRetriever` takes a `VectorStoreInfo` (a content description plus `MetadataInfo` entries with name, type and description) and infers a query string, metadata filters and `top_k`.
The figure below runs the five filters on eight toy profiles. Watch which constraint removes whom, and pay attention to Hana in the last step.

blocks.title: Five hard filters applied to eight toy profiles

scenes.caption: Eight toy profiles indexed with canonical fields (sr = senior, md = mid, swe = software engineer, ds = data scientist, +r = open to remote). Before any filter, all eight are eligible.
Filter 1, title_id = software engineer: Gus is a data scientist, so Gus is removed even though the profile mentions Rust. Similarity search could still rank Gus high.
Filter 2, seniority = senior: Chen (mid) is removed. Words in the query became exact, unscored yes or no checks.
Filter 3, skills contains rust: Dara (Java only) is removed.
Filter 4, (city = Berlin) OR (open to remote): Fay is in Hamburg and not remote, so Fay goes. Ben stays: Ben is in Munich but open to remote, which is what remote ok means here.
Filter 5, salary below 150000: Eli (165k) goes, and so does Hana, whose profile has no salary at all. A range filter drops documents with no value for the field. Two of eight remain: Ana and Ben.

blocks.prompt: Hana is a senior Rust engineer in Berlin, open to remote, but the profile has no salary field. Will a plain range filter `salary < 150000` keep that profile?
blocks.reveal: No. In Elasticsearch a `range` query only matches documents that have an indexed value in range, and a field that is `null` or absent has no indexed value. Hana silently disappears. Whether that is right is a product decision (maybe the candidate would accept 120k), and lesson 3 shows how to keep documents with a missing value when you want to.

blocks.md: The LLM never touches the documents. It only translates the query into a filter object. Exact enforcement is done by the search engine, which is cheap, deterministic and testable.

blocks.question: Why should *under 150k* become a range filter instead of being left in the text that gets embedded?
options: Embedding models cannot read numbers at all, so the number is ignored
Range filters are faster to score than vectors, which is the main reason
Similarity is a soft score, so a 165k profile can still outrank a 140k one; a filter excludes it with certainty
Keyword search would match it exactly, so either approach works
blocks.explain: Embeddings do see the digits, but similarity mixes them with every other token into one soft score, so nothing guarantees the bound. A range filter is a yes or no test per document. Keyword search matches the string 150k, not the numeric relation below 150000.

blocks.question: LangChain's default few-shot prompt includes the question *What are songs that were not published on Spotify* for a data source whose only fields are artist, length and genre. What filter does the example answer give?
options: and(ne("platform", "Spotify"))
NO_FILTER, because no field records the platform
not(contain("artist", "Spotify"))
It refuses to answer the query
blocks.explain: The example answer is query "" with filter NO_FILTER. The prompt also instructs the model that filters may only refer to attributes that exist. Inventing a platform field would produce a query the store cannot run, or one that silently matches nothing.

lessons.title: Designing the filter schema: enums, ranges and nulls

blocks.md: From the prerequisite course: with strict structured outputs, a constrained decoder masks every token that would break the JSON schema, so the output always parses and has the right shape. That guarantee is about **shape**. Whether `seniority: "senior"` is what the user meant is still up to you, and most of that is decided by how you design the schema.

Rules that work well for a filter object:

- **Closed, small sets** (seniority, employment type) become an `enum`. The decoder cannot emit a value outside it.
- **Open, large sets** (cities, job titles, skills, companies) stay free strings. The model copies what the user wrote and your code maps it to an ID (lesson 3). OpenAI documents a cap on the total number of enum values in a schema, and a giant enum also costs prompt tokens on every call.
- **Ranges** become an object of nullable bounds that mirror the target engine (`gte`, `lte`, `lt`), so *under*, *at most* and *at least* keep their exact meaning.
- **Absent means null.** In strict mode OpenAI requires every field to be listed as required, and optional values are emulated with a union with `null`.
- **Negation gets its own fields** (`skills_not`), and leftover words go to a `text` field.

blocks.title: Filling the schema for the Berlin query
blocks.code:
{
  "name": "candidate_filters",
  "strict": true,
  "schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "additionalProperties": false,
    "required": ["role", "seniority", "skills", "skills_not",
                 "locations", "remote_ok", "salary", "text"],
    "properties": {
      "role": { "type": ["string", "null"],
        "description": "Job title as written, e.g. backend developer" },
      "seniority": { "anyOf": [ { "type": "null" },
        { "type": "string",
          "enum": ["junior", "mid", "senior", "staff", "principal"] } ] },
      "skills": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" },
        "description": "Skills the candidate must ALL have" },
      "skills_not": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" },
        "description": "Skills the user excluded (not, no, without)" },
      "locations": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" },
        "description": "Cities, any of them is acceptable" },
      "remote_ok": { "type": ["boolean", "null"] },
      "salary": { "anyOf": [ { "type": "null" },
        { "type": "object", "additionalProperties": false,
          "required": ["gte", "lte", "lt", "currency"],
          "properties": {
            "gte": { "type": ["integer", "null"] },
            "lte": { "type": ["integer", "null"] },
            "lt":  { "type": ["integer", "null"] },
            "currency": { "anyOf": [ { "type": "null" },
              { "type": "string", "enum": ["EUR", "USD", "GBP"] } ] } } } ] },
      "text": { "type": "string",
        "description": "Words left over for relevance ranking" }
    }
  }
}

scenes.caption: Strict mode: every property is listed in required and additionalProperties is false, so the decoder cannot skip a field or invent one. Optional means nullable, not absent.
role is an open vocabulary, so it is a plain string copied from the query. Mapping it to an ID is done later by code. Here the model writes engineers in singular form.
seniority is a small closed set, so it is an enum: the decoder can only emit one of five values or null. senior maps directly.
Separate include and exclude arrays give negation a place to go. Nothing is excluded in this query, so skills_not is an empty array rather than null.
Cities are thousands of values, too many for an enum, so they stay strings. remote ok sets remote_ok to true; the compiler decides how it combines with the city list.
under 150k becomes lt = 150000 with the other bounds null. The query names no currency, so currency is null: the model must not guess, and code fills in an assumption it can show the user.
Every word was consumed by a filter, so the residual text is empty. A query like ... with distributed systems experience would leave that phrase here for relevance ranking.

blocks.md: A required, non-nullable field such as `salary_max: integer` forces the model to produce a number even when the user said nothing about salary. Constrained decoding guarantees *some* integer, so you get an invented bound (for example 0, or a number copied from a few-shot example) and a filter that silently removes good results.

Descriptions are part of the schema. LangChain's `AttributeInfo` and LlamaIndex's `MetadataInfo` both carry a free-text `description`, and the model reads it. Put conventions there: salary is annual, 150k means 150000, *under* uses `lt` and *at most* uses `lte`, `locations` is any-of while `skills` is all-of. Add two or three few-shot examples (including one with negation and one with no filters at all), as LangChain's default prompt does.

blocks.prompt: The user types *data scientist berlin max 120k EUR*. Which salary bound should the parser fill?
blocks.reveal: `lte: 120000` with `currency: "EUR"`. *Max* includes the boundary, so it is `lte`; *under 120k* would be `lt`. Keeping all three bounds in the schema means the compiler can pass them straight into an Elasticsearch `range` query, which has the same `gte`, `lte` and `lt` parameters, without anyone re-deriving the boundary rule.

blocks.question: Which representation of the city should the LLM output for an index with 40000 distinct city IDs?
options: An enum listing all 40000 city IDs so decoding is constrained
The city as a free string, mapped to a canonical ID by a lookup in code
An integer GeoNames ID, since models memorize popular IDs
Nothing: leave cities in the residual text for the embedding to handle
blocks.explain: A huge enum exceeds documented schema limits and costs tokens on every request, and models do not reliably know arbitrary IDs, so an invented ID would look valid. Leaving the city in text turns a hard constraint back into a soft one. Extract the surface string and normalize it deterministically.

blocks.question: A team's schema has `"min_years": {"type": "integer"}` in strict mode. For the query *rust engineers in Berlin*, what is the most likely problem?
options: The request is rejected because integers are unsupported in strict mode
The field is omitted from the output, which breaks the parser
The model emits null, which the compiler treats as no filter
The model must emit some integer, so it may invent a minimum that filters out valid candidates
blocks.explain: Strict mode requires every field and enforces the type, and integer does not admit null. The decoder must produce digits, so the model makes up a value. Declare the field as integer or null and compile null to no clause.

lessons.title: From extracted strings to canonical IDs and a bool query

blocks.md: The parser output for our query has `role: "engineer"` and `locations: ["Berlin"]`. The index stores `title_id: "t:swe"` and `location_id: "geo:berlin"`. **Normalization** maps every extracted surface string to the **canonical ID** your index uses, and it should be ordinary code: a dictionary lookup first, then a similarity search over the vocabulary for misses.

scenes.caption: The LLM copied what the user wrote. None of these strings equals the value stored in the index, so a term filter on any of them would match nothing.
Step 1 is cheap and deterministic: lowercase, trim punctuation and country suffixes, then look the result up in an alias table built from your own data. This resolves most real traffic.

Step 2 for misses: fuzzy or embedding nearest neighbor over the canonical vocabulary, accepted only above a similarity threshold. Gotham has no close match, so it must not become a hard filter (lesson 4).

blocks.md: Why not ask the LLM for the ID directly? It cannot know arbitrary IDs it was never shown, and a made-up ID such as `geo:berlin-de` passes every format check. If you want the model to choose, retrieve the top few candidate IDs for the string first and offer only those as an enum for that request. Either way, an unknown value is an event to handle, never something to filter on.

Next, a small compiler turns the normalized object into Elasticsearch Query DSL. The `bool` query has four clause types: `must` and `should` contribute to the score; `filter` and `must_not` run in **filter context**, where scoring is ignored and clauses are considered for caching. Hard constraints therefore belong in `filter`. Inside it, `term` tests one exact stored value, `terms` any of several, and `range` numeric bounds; `match` is scored full-text search. LangChain's `ElasticsearchTranslator` makes the same mapping from its own language: `and` to must, `or` to should, `not` to must_not, `eq` to term (on the `.keyword` subfield for strings) and `gt gte lt lte` to range.

blocks.title: Where each field lands in the bool query

scenes.caption: Exact constraints go to filter: a yes or no test with no score, and Elasticsearch caches frequently used filters. term needs a keyword field; on an analyzed text field, use match instead.
Berlin OR remote is a disjunction. It becomes its own nested bool with should clauses and minimum_should_match 1, then sits inside filter like any other test.
Salary bounds pass straight through as a range query, and excluded skills go to must_not, which also runs in filter context.
Only the residual text is scored, with a match query in must. With an empty text the query is pure filtering and every hit scores the same; add a sort or a recency signal if order matters.

blocks.caption: The compiler is plain code: deterministic, unit-testable and identical for every query.
Its output for the Berlin query, produced by running the function above on the normalized filter object.

blocks.md: The `minimum_should_match` default depends on context. In Elasticsearch it is 1 only when the bool has `should` clauses and no `must` or `filter` clauses; otherwise it is 0, and the should clauses become optional score boosts. Put Berlin and remote as bare should clauses next to a filter list and *every* city passes.

Missing values need an explicit policy. The `exists` query matches documents with an indexed value; a field that is `null` or `[]` has none. To keep Hana, whose salary is unknown, compile the bound as a nested bool with should `[range salary_eur lt 150000, bool must_not exists salary_eur]` and minimum_should_match 1. On our toy profiles that returns Ana, Ben and Hana instead of Ana and Ben.

blocks.question: A developer moves the location clauses to the top-level bool: `{"bool": {"filter": [title, seniority, skill, salary], "should": [Berlin, remote]}}`. What happens to Fay in Hamburg (not remote, salary 125k)?
options: The profile is returned: with filter clauses present, should defaults to minimum_should_match 0, so location only affects the score
The profile is excluded, because should always requires at least one clause to match
Elasticsearch rejects the query because should cannot be combined with filter
The profile is excluded, because filter clauses are evaluated after should clauses
blocks.explain: The docs state the default is 1 only when there are should clauses and no must or filter clauses. Here filter exists, so the default is 0 and the should clauses only add score. Nest the disjunction in its own bool, or set minimum_should_match explicitly.

blocks.question: The user asks for candidates who know Rust and Go. A compiler emits `{"terms": {"skills": ["rust", "go"]}}`. What does it return?
options: Only profiles listing both rust and go
Profiles listing rust and go in that order
Profiles listing rust or go or both
Nothing, because terms needs a text field
blocks.explain: terms returns documents that contain one or more of the listed exact terms, so it is any-of. All-of needs one term clause per skill inside filter, which is what the compiler above does. Mixing these up is easy because both read naturally as a list of skills.

blocks.md: Real queries are underspecified. *Under 150k* in Berlin does not name a currency or a period. *Remote ok* could mean Berlin or remote, or remote only. *Lead rust developer* might be a title or a seniority level. *Experienced* has no number at all. The parser cannot resolve these from the text, so the system needs written **policies**.

A workable pattern:

- Write each convention into the field description and one few-shot example (remote ok means city OR remote; lead maps to staff).
- Let the model return `null` where the query is silent (currency), and have code fill a **recorded assumption** (EUR, because the city is in Germany).
- Show parsed filters and assumptions as chips the user can remove. A visible wrong guess is cheap; an invisible one loses candidates.

**Negation** is the classic weak spot of semantic parsing. *Python but not R*, *who don't do javascript* and *java (not javascript)* all need the excluded value in `skills_not` and nowhere else. Two failure modes are common: dropping the negation (R lands in `skills`) and flipping it (javascript becomes required). In lesson 5's labeled set, three of the four queries with a negation are parsed wrong, while the fourth (*not java*) is right.

A cheap guard: if the query contains a negation cue (not, no, without, except, don't) but every exclude list is empty, re-ask with a negation few-shot example or fall back to keyword search. This is a heuristic, so measure its effect on your own labeled set.

nodes.label:
Relax one filter
and tell the user

scenes.caption: Strict decoding guarantees parseable JSON, but OpenAI documents that a refusal can come back instead of schema output, and any call can time out. Both go straight to keyword search.
Semantic checks catch what the schema cannot: an unknown city, gte above lte, the same skill in skills and skills_not. Unknown values move into the residual text instead of becoming filters.
Filters can be individually right and jointly impossible. On zero hits, relax the least certain filter (often an assumed currency or an inferred bound), rerun, and show which filter was dropped.
Results come back with the parsed filters shown as editable chips, so a wrong parse costs the user one click instead of a silent miss.

blocks.prompt: For *senior rust engineers in Hamburg, remote ok, under 100k* the strict filter returns zero of the eight toy profiles. Which relaxation should run first: dropping seniority, dropping the salary bound, or keeping profiles with no salary value?
blocks.reveal: Keeping profiles with no salary value. It violates nothing the user said; the profile simply lacks data. On the toy set it recovers Hana. Dropping a stated constraint (the salary bound returns Fay, Ben and Hana) should come later and be announced. Dropping seniority alone would return no one here, because every remaining failure is about salary.

blocks.title: Hits on the toy profiles as filters are relaxed

scenes.caption: Query: senior rust engineers in Hamburg, remote ok, under 100k. Fay (Hamburg, 125k), Ben (remote, 130k) and Hana (remote, no salary) all fail the salary bound, so the strict query returns nothing.
Keeping profiles with no salary value (the exists trick from lesson 3) recovers Hana. This is the gentlest relaxation: no stated constraint is violated.
Dropping the salary bound returns Fay, Ben and Hana. Each now violates a stated constraint or has none, so the UI must say so (for example: no matches under 100k; showing the closest).

blocks.md: Never silently drop a filter the user asked for. A validator that deletes an unknown value and runs the rest turns *rust engineers in Gotham* into *rust engineers anywhere*, and the user believes the results are in Gotham.

blocks.question: The parser returns `locations: ["Gotham"]`, and normalization finds no city above the similarity threshold. What is the best action?
options: Filter on the string Gotham anyway, since the user asked for it
Drop the location filter silently and run the other filters
Ask the LLM again until it returns a known city
Move Gotham into the residual text, run the other filters, and tell the user the city was not recognized
blocks.explain: Filtering on an unknown ID returns nothing, retrying invites a hallucinated substitute, and silent dropping changes the meaning. Moving the word into scored text keeps it as soft evidence, and the message lets the user correct it.

blocks.question: Which parse is correct for *backend people who know java (not javascript) in hamburg*?
options: skills: [java], skills_not: [javascript]
skills: [java, javascript], skills_not: []
skills: [], skills_not: [java, javascript]
skills: [java], skills_not: [], text: not javascript
blocks.explain: Java is required and JavaScript is excluded. Option two is the dropped-negation error that appears in the lesson 5 set. Putting the exclusion in text makes it a scored match, which would actually boost profiles that mention JavaScript.

lessons.title: Evaluating the parser with exact match per field

blocks.md: You cannot improve what you do not measure. Build a **labeled set**: real queries from your logs, each with a gold filter object written in canonical IDs. Score the parser field by field, because a single pass or fail per query hides *which* field breaks, and different fields fail for different reasons.

Text-to-SQL research faced the same question. The Spider benchmark (Yu et al., 2018) reports **component matching**: each SQL clause is decomposed into a set of parts and compared with the gold set, so order does not matter. **Exact matching** counts a query correct only if every component matches. Spider also notes that execution accuracy can give false positives, when a wrong query happens to return the same rows. Spider left out condition values; for filter parsing the values (Berlin, 150000) are most of the job.

blocks.caption: Per-field accuracy and whole-object exact match. Lists are compared as sets, and null equals null, so correctly leaving a field empty counts as a hit.

blocks.md: Our toy set has 10 queries and 7 fields. q1 is the Berlin query; the others include *backend devs in munich who know go and kubernetes* (q2), *data scientists in Hamburg with python but not R* (q3), *junior java developers in berlin or hamburg* (q5), *lead rust developer, remote-friendly, berlin* (q9) and *backend people who know java (not javascript) in hamburg under 100k* (q10).
The predictions in this lesson are hand-written to show typical error types. They are not measurements of any model. Use the method, not the numbers.

blocks.title: Per-field exact match on 10 labeled queries

scenes.caption: Comparing the parser's strings directly with the gold labels: 52 of 70 fields match and only 1 of 10 queries is fully right. role scores 0.4 because engineer, developer and SRE are not the canonical label.
After normalization (aliases, case, München to geo:munich) the same predictions score 61 of 70, and 4 of 10 queries are fully right. Normalization fixes formatting, not understanding.

The errors that remain are semantic. q3, q7 and q10 break both skill columns (negation dropped or flipped), q5 misses Hamburg in berlin or hamburg, q9 maps lead to senior, and q6 adds remote_ok nobody asked for.

blocks.title: Field accuracy before and after normalization

scenes.caption: Raw string comparison. Low scores here mostly measure formatting differences: role 0.4, skills 0.6, locations 0.7.
After normalization role rises to 1.0 and locations to 0.9. skills and skills_not stay at 0.7: those errors are negation, which no lookup table can fix.

blocks.md: Summary after normalization: micro accuracy over all 70 fields is 0.871 (up from 0.743), and whole-object exact match is 0.4 (up from 0.1). Counting only non-empty slots, the parser filled 34 slots correctly, 6 slots that are wrong or should be empty, and missed 7 gold slots, so slot precision is 0.85 and recall is 0.83.

Errors are not equal. A **spurious** filter (q6's remote_ok, q7's required javascript) removes good results and the user never sees them. A **missing** filter only returns extra results the user can see and skip. Track precision and recall of slots separately and weight spurious filters as the worse error.

blocks.question: A parser gets each of 7 fields right 90 percent of the time, independently. Roughly what whole-object exact match should you expect?
options: 90 percent, the same as each field
about 63 percent
about 48 percent
about 10 percent
blocks.explain: Exact match needs all 7 right: 0.9 to the power 7 is about 0.478. This is why object exact match looks harsh and why per-field scores are needed to see what to fix. Real field errors are correlated (a confusing query breaks several), which usually makes EM a bit better than the independent estimate.

blocks.question: Instead of labeling filter objects, a teammate proposes to score the parser by whether the compiled query returns the same documents as the gold query on today's index. What is the main risk?
options: It is too slow to run on 10 queries
False positives: on a small or sparse index, a wrong filter can return the same documents, for example both return zero hits
It cannot handle negation at all
It requires a GPU for every evaluation run
blocks.explain: This is execution accuracy, and Spider notes it can report a semantically different query as correct when results coincide. Two wrong-for-different-reasons queries that both return nothing look identical. Use it as a complement to field-level matching, not a replacement.

lessons.title: Latency budgets, caching and parallel fallback

blocks.md: A search box has a latency budget, and an LLM call can be most of it. The figures below use an **assumed** model (cache 2 ms, parse 450 ms, normalize 3 ms, filtered query 30 ms, keyword query 40 ms) to show the structure of the tradeoff; substitute your own measured numbers.

blocks.title: Request timelines under an assumed latency model

scenes.caption: Cache miss, sequential. Assumed: cache 2 ms, LLM parse 450 ms, normalize 3 ms, filtered query 30 ms. Total 485 ms, and the LLM is 93 percent of it. Simplified: real parse latency varies with model, prompt length and load.
Cache hit: the parsed and normalized filter for this exact normalized query is already stored. 2 ms lookup plus 30 ms query gives 32 ms.

Speculative keyword search: start a 40 ms BM25 query on the raw text in parallel with the parse. The parse returns at 452 ms, inside a 600 ms deadline, so the keyword results are discarded and the filtered query runs.
A slow tail call: the parse would take 900 ms. At the 600 ms deadline the API returns the keyword results it already has. The user gets a worse answer on time instead of a better one late.

blocks.md:
Three levers:

1. **Cache the parse, not the results.** Key on the normalized query string (lowercased, whitespace collapsed) plus the schema version and vocabulary version. Results change as the index changes; the parse of *senior rust engineers in berlin* does not, until you change the schema or the dictionaries.
2. **Run keyword search in parallel** with a deadline, and return it if the parse is late or fails.
3. **Make the miss cheaper.** Put the static part of the prompt (instructions, field descriptions, examples) first and the user query last: OpenAI's prompt caching reuses a matching prefix, with a documented minimum prompt length. For fine-tuned models, OpenAI also documents extra latency on the first request with a new schema, one more reason to keep the schema stable rather than regenerating it per request.

blocks.title: Mean latency vs parse-cache hit rate

scenes.caption: Same assumed model: hit costs 32 ms, miss costs 35 ms plus the parse. With a 450 ms parse, mean latency falls from 485 ms at 0 percent hits to 258.5 ms at 50 percent and 167.9 ms at 70 percent.

With a slower 1200 ms parse the line is steeper: each point of hit rate saves more. The mean hides the tail, though: misses still pay the full parse, so p99 is set by misses unless a deadline caps it. The marked points are still the 450 ms values.

blocks.title: Idealized hit rate of a top-K query cache

scenes.caption: Model: N = 1 million distinct queries with Zipf (s = 1) popularity, caching the K most popular. Hit rate is H(K) / H(N) with H(n) about ln n + 0.577: 0.36 at K = 100, 0.52 at 1000, 0.68 at 10000. Simplified: measure your own log; tails are often heavier.

With 100 million distinct queries the same caches hit less, because more traffic sits in the tail. Parse caching helps most for head queries, which is also where the hard filters repeat. Marked points still show N = 1 million.

blocks.md: Not every query needs the LLM. A one-word query or an exact product code has no constraints to extract. A cheap gate (length, presence of numbers, location or negation words) can send those straight to keyword search, and you can check the gate's misses against your labeled set.
Design for the miss: the parse cache sets the mean, the deadline and keyword fallback set the tail.

blocks.question: Which cache key is safest for storing parsed filter objects?
options: The raw query string exactly as typed
The normalized query string alone
The normalized query plus the user's session ID
The normalized query plus the schema version and vocabulary version
blocks.explain: Raw strings fragment the cache on case and spacing. Without versions, a schema or dictionary change keeps serving stale parses (an old field name, a city ID that was split). The session ID would make the cache nearly useless, since the parse does not depend on who asked.

blocks.question: To benefit from prompt prefix caching, where should the user's query go in the parser prompt?
options: At the end, after the instructions, field descriptions and examples
At the start, so the model reads it first
In the middle, between instructions and examples
It does not matter, caching hashes the whole prompt
blocks.explain: Caching reuses a matching prefix, so everything identical across requests should come first and the part that changes every time should come last. A query at the start changes the prefix on every request and nothing is reused.
